what_changed:
President Trump ended the Biden-era LNG export pause on his first day in office, January 20, 2025. DOE, under Secretary Chris Wright, then issued a series of LNG export authorizations. CP2 LNG received a conditional authorization in March 2025, followed in May 2025 by FERC's order reaffirming its approval of the facility's siting and construction. DOE issued CP2 LNG's final non-FTA export authorization, DOE/FECM Order No. 5264-A, on October 21, 2025 (announced the next day), permitting exports of up to 3.96 billion cubic feet per day. Assistant Secretary of the Office of Fossil Energy Kyle Haustveit said finalizing the authorization would 'enable secure and reliable American energy access for our allies.' DOE stated **the Trump administration has authorized more than 13.8 Bcf/d of LNG exports in total since ending the pause, exceeding the export volume of the world's second-largest LNG supplier**. The same week as CP2's final authorization, Trump administration officials and Qatar sent a joint letter pressuring the European Union to roll back new EU climate and human-rights due-diligence rules, arguing they threaten LNG imports and 'European economic stability.' That letter is a related but separate diplomatic pressure campaign, not a U.S. domestic regulatory action, and is not otherwise covered here.

Update 2026-10-22: On August 25, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit denied the petitions for review brought by environmental groups and commercial fishermen and upheld FERC's authorization of the CP2 terminal and its CP Express pipeline. A separate challenge to DOE's export orders, filed in the D.C. Circuit by Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council on February 17, 2026, remained pending as of CP2 LNG's October 1, 2026 progress report to DOE. DOE formally denied the groups' rehearing request on March 26, 2026.

rule_name: Copper Rule (EPA emissions standards for primary copper smelters, finalized May 13, 2024 under Clean Air Act Section 112)

glance.what: Exempted an Arizona copper smelter from 2024 toxic-emissions limits for up to two years

section_summaries.what_changed: Trump used a rare national-security power to exempt Freeport's Arizona copper smelter, which asked by email, from 2024 toxic-emissions limits for two years; Sen. Kelly has pressed EPA to undo it.

what_changed:
On October 24, 2025, President Trump signed Proclamation 10987 (published in the Federal Register on November 3, 2025), granting Freeport-McMoRan's Arizona smelter a two-year exemption from the Copper Rule's compliance deadlines. He used Clean Air Act Section 112(i)(4), a rarely-used provision that lets the President exempt a stationary source from a Section 112 standard for up to two years if compliance technology is unavailable and the exemption serves the national security interest. The proclamation stated 'the technology to implement the Copper Rule is not available' in a 'commercially viable form' to meet the rule's deadlines, and that preserving domestic smelting capacity was essential to critical-minerals access in a crisis. It added that imposing the requirements on 'such a limited and already strained domestic industry risks accelerating further closures.' Freeport-McMoRan said the exemption 'provides needed time to assess and plan for appropriate regulatory reconsideration of the Copper Rule.' Rio Tinto's Utah smelter was not affected: the company had already invested in emissions-capture equipment to comply. This is the same Section 112(i)(4) mechanism, and, per ProPublica reporting, the same email-based exemption-request process EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin invited industry to use, that this tracker's separate ethylene-oxide sterilizer entry documents. There it was applied to exempt 40 sterilization facilities (roughly 45% of that industry) from a different Section 112 rule. Copper smelting is a second, independently documented industry where the same national-security exemption authority was invoked to delay compliance with toxic-emissions standards.

Update 2026-10-24: A joint investigation by ProPublica and Gray Media's National Team, reported by Arizona's Family in April 2026, found that Freeport-McMoRan was able to get the exemption "by sending a few emails," using an email address records show EPA set up under the Trump administration. Without it, the Miami smelter would have had to install an additional filter, a baghouse, to capture more toxic emissions, including lead, arsenic and chromium; the Utah smelter has already installed one. In its exemption request Freeport said the filter would cost more than $300 million; under the Biden administration EPA put the cost at about $60 million. At an April 29, 2026 Senate Environment and Public Works Committee hearing on EPA's proposed fiscal 2027 budget, Sen. Mark Kelly, citing the investigation's finding that the facility emits 12 tons of lead and 13 tons of arsenic a year, asked EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to commit to working to undo the exemption. Zeldin said it was the first time he had heard about the issue and that his role on these exemptions "has been to receive and transmit pursuant to the statute." Freeport says the exemption gives EPA time to reconsider aspects of the rule, a review it says "is underway now," and does not authorize any increase in emissions.

what_changed:
On February 24, 2026, EPA published a proposed rule, the 'Common Sense Approach to Chemical Accident Prevention,' that would rescind or substantially scale back most of the 2024 SCCAP requirements. Key rollbacks: eliminating STAA requirements for existing facilities in the two highest-risk sectors (chemical manufacturing and petroleum/coal products, NAICS 324/325), limiting STAA to newly built processes only; rescinding most third-party audit requirements (with a narrower option requiring audits only for facilities with 2+ accidents in 5 years); eliminating the requirement to share chemical hazard information directly with the public on request, relying instead on EPA's more limited online Data Tool; and rescinding several worker-protection provisions including anonymous reporting, stop-work authority, and mandatory workers' rights training. EPA frames the changes as realigning RMP with OSHA's existing Process Safety Management standard and removing 'duplicative' requirements. The proposal followed a March 2025 EPA announcement that it would reconsider the SCCAP rule, itself prompted by Executive Orders 14148 and 14154 directing agencies to rescind Biden-era regulatory actions. The proposal set an April 10, 2026 comment deadline; on April 2, 2026, citing stakeholders' requests, EPA extended it by 31 days, and the comment period closed May 11, 2026. In a March 2025 motion asking the D.C. Circuit to pause litigation over the 2024 rule, EPA said it aimed to publish a final rule in late 2026.

Update 2026-10-06: EPA's 2026 regulatory agenda listed a September 2026 target for the final rule. That month passed without a final rule being published, and the proposal remains pending.
